newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Ireland thrives but concerns ahead.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Ireland thrives but concerns ahead.

text.p: Irish government bonds have been thriving amid economic restructuring and enthusiasm towards a single European currency but investors must not get complacent, analysts said on Friday.
The country received a reward for its economic turnaround on Thursday when Moody's Investors Service raised its foreign-currency sovereign ceiling for bond and bank deposits.
But the link between sterling and the punt, and uncertainty over Britain's attitude towards European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), will cast shadows over the debt market.
"At this stage, I would be quite cautious," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at BankAmerica in London.

"Both the background to the Irish economy and fact that we have uncertainty due to the link in with sterling, will mean spreads will remain relatively high versus Germany and the Irish bond market will be outperformed by hard core Europe at least for the time being."
He said the 10-year Irish bond yield spread against Bunds was currently around 85 basis points and would probably move out towards 100 basis points. It began 1997 around 92 basis points.
But Paul Horne, chief international economist at Smith Barney in Paris, was more bullish for Irish bonds.
"Ireland is one of the great success stories," he said. "The Moody's upgrade is a well merited Valentine's Day persent, but there are a couple of warnings."
Moody's raised Ireland's foreign-currency sovereign ceilings for bonds and bank deposits to Aa1 from Aa2.

Analysts said the link between Irish and Britsh currencies meant sterling strength was pulling the punt higher, and could damage Ireland's chances for qualifying for the first wave of European and Economic Monetary Union (EMU).

"The background to the Irish market in general is quite confusing. There is an ongoing policy dilemma for the Irish central bank as to what they should be doing with interest rates," said Hawkins. "At some point they are probably going to bite the bullet and see the Irish punt weakening."
The punt is currently in a 15 percent fluctuation band within the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM). Prior to European currency crises of 1992/93, it was in a 2.25 percent ERM band.
Under old ERM rules, most currencies were within that narrow band, except for Britain and Spain which had 6.0 percent bands.
Hawkins said authorities might want to push the punt down to within a 6.0 percent band initially, then aim for 2.25 percent.
In order to achieve this, Hawkins said an interest rate cut would probably be needed and this was not justified by the domestic fundamentals, given buoyant consumer spending.
Such a move would lead to some steepening of the yield curve in the short term, he added..

David Crofts, in international bonds sales at Williams de Broe in London, also said an interest rate cut was unlikely because credit rate growth was too strong. He said a realignment of the punt was also unlikely to happen.
"That is extremely unlikely, particulary as it would harm the farmers and reduce their incomes in an election year, which wouldn't be very clever politically," he said.
Horne said he was not overly concerned about sterling strength. He expected the currency to rise further but fall sharply in the second half of the year, taking the punt with it.
What was more of a concern was the attitude of a future British government towards participation in EMU, Horne said. Elections have to take place in Britain by May 22.

"If the new British government makes it very clear that the UK will go into EMU in the first round, there is a risk that investors will calculate the UK in EMU as the best place to have a competitive economy," said Horne. "Therefore sterling might stay higher...and the punt along with it."
--Deepthi Wickremasinghe, Bonds Unit +44 171 542 4041
